topics.title: 1.2 Arrow Functions & Callback Handlers
topics.description: Use concise arrow function syntax to build inline event handlers and filter operations.
topics.lessonMarkdown:
# 1.2 Arrow Functions & Callback Handlers ## Before React: understand functions A function is a reusable block of code. ```javascript function add(a, b) { return a + b; } console.log(add(2, 3)); // 5 ``` React uses functions everywhere: - components are functions - event handlers are functions - `map()` callbacks are functions - `filter()` callbacks are functions - `reduce()` callbacks are functions So learning functions well makes React much easier. --- ## 1. Regular function syntax ```javascript function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}`; } ``` A function can: - receive input through parameters - perform work - return a value ```javascript function square(number) { return number * number; } ``` --- ## 2. Arrow function syntax The same function can be written as: ```javascript const square = (number) => { return number * number; }; ``` Because the body contains only one returned expression, it can be shorter: ```javascript const square = number => number * number; ``` All three examples represent the same basic calculation. --- ## 3. Parameters and parentheses One parameter: ```javascript const double = n => n * 2; ``` Two parameters: ```javascript const add = (a, b) => a + b; ``` No parameters: ```javascript const sayHello = () => "Hello"; ``` Multiple statements: ```javascript const calculate = price => { const tax = price * 0.08; return price + tax; }; ``` --- ## 4. Returning an object from an arrow function This is a common beginner trap. This is **not** an object return: ```javascript const makeUser = () => { name: "Anu" }; ``` The braces are interpreted as a function body. Use parentheses: ```javascript const makeUser = () => ({ name: "Anu" }); ``` --- ## 5. What is a callback? A callback is a function passed to another function so that it can be called later. ```javascript function processUser(name, callback) { callback(name); } processUser("Anu", name => { console.log(`Welcome ${name}`); }); ``` Array methods use callbacks heavily. ```javascript const numbers = [1, 2, 3]; numbers.map(number => number * 2); ``` Here: ```text map = the function doing the iteration number => number * 2 = the callback ``` --- ## 6. Arrow functions in React events React event handlers receive functions. Correct: ```jsx ``` Notice that we pass a function. Incorrect: ```jsx ``` The second version calls the function during rendering instead of waiting for the click. When arguments are needed, the arrow function gives you a small wrapper: ```jsx ``` --- ## 7. Arrow functions and list rendering A very common React pattern is: ```jsx const users = [ { id: 1, name: "Anu", active: true }, { id: 2, name: "Ravi", active: false } ]; const activeUsers = users.filter(user => user.active); ``` Then: ```jsx
    {activeUsers.map(user => (
  • {user.name}
    • ))}
``` The flow is: ```text users ↓ filter() active users ↓ map() JSX elements ↓ screen ``` --- ## 8. Lexical `this` Arrow functions do not create their own `this`; they use `this` from the surrounding scope. This is important when reading older JavaScript code, although modern React function components usually do not need `this` at all. For React beginners, focus on this practical rule: > Arrow functions are concise function expressions and are excellent for callbacks and event handlers. --- ## 9. Read this line character by character ```javascript const activeUsers = users.filter(user => user.active); ``` - `const activeUsers` creates a variable. - `users` is an array. - `.filter(...)` examines every item. - `user => user.active` is the callback. - returning `true` keeps an item. - returning `false` removes it. Equivalent longer form: ```javascript const activeUsers = users.filter(function (user) { return user.active; }); ``` --- ## Example: event + callback ```jsx import { useState } from "react"; export default function App() { const [message, setMessage] = useState("Waiting"); const activate = () => { setMessage("Online"); }; return (

{message}

); } ``` Inline style: ```jsx ``` Both are valid. --- ## Example: filter + map ```jsx const courses = [ { id: 1, title: "HTML", published: true }, { id: 2, title: "React", published: false }, { id: 3, title: "JavaScript", published: true } ]; function CourseList() { return (
    {courses .filter(course => course.published) .map(course => (
  • {course.title}
    • ))}
); } ``` Only HTML and JavaScript appear. --- ## Beginner mistakes ### Mistake 1: calling the handler immediately ```jsx onClick={handleSave()} // ❌ ``` Use: ```jsx onClick={handleSave} // ✅ ``` Or, when passing arguments: ```jsx onClick={() => handleSave(id)} // ✅ ``` ### Mistake 2: forgetting `return` ```javascript const double = number => { number * 2; }; ``` This returns `undefined`. Correct: ```javascript const double = number => { return number * 2; }; ``` Or: ```javascript const double = number => number * 2; ``` ### Mistake 3: using `filter()` for transformation `filter()` decides which items stay. `map()` creates a changed representation of each item. ```text filter → same kind of array, fewer items map → same number of items, transformed values ``` --- ## Mini challenge What does this return? ```javascript const names = ["Anu", "Ravi", "Maya"]; const result = names .filter(name => name.length >= 4) .map(name => name.toUpperCase()); ``` Answer: ```javascript ["RAVI", "MAYA"] ``` Further reading: - React: Responding to Events — https://react.dev/learn/responding-to-events - W3Schools: React JSX — https://www.w3schools.com/react/react_jsx.asp - Scrimba: React introduction — https://docs.scrimba.com/react/introduction - GeeksforGeeks: React Components — https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/reactjs/reactjs-components/

topics.title: 1.3 Array Transformations (.map, .filter, .reduce)
topics.description: Transform raw data arrays into dynamic UI elements and aggregated metrics.
topics.lessonMarkdown:
# 1.3 Array Transformations (.map, .filter, .reduce) ## Why arrays matter in React Real applications receive collections: ```javascript const students = [...]; const products = [...]; const courses = [...]; const messages = [...]; ``` React often needs to turn those arrays into UI. The three methods you will use constantly are: ```text map → transform each item filter → keep matching items reduce → combine many items into one result ``` --- ## 1. `map()` `map()` creates a new array with one result for every original item. ```javascript const numbers = [1, 2, 3]; const doubled = numbers.map(number => number * 2); console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6] ``` The original array remains unchanged. ```text [1, 2, 3] ↓ map(x => x * 2) [2, 4, 6] ``` ### React example ```jsx const skills = ["HTML", "CSS", "React"]; function SkillList() { return (
    {skills.map(skill => (
  • {skill}
    • ))}
); } ``` ### Why does React need `key`? When rendering a list, React needs a stable identity for each item. ```jsx
  • {student.name}
    • ``` Prefer a real stable identifier from the data. Avoid generating a new random key during every render. --- ## 2. `filter()` `filter()` keeps elements for which the callback returns `true`. ```javascript const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; const evenNumbers = numbers.filter(number => number % 2 === 0); console.log(evenNumbers); // [2, 4] ``` Think: ```text keep it? yes → include keep it? no → discard ``` ### React example ```jsx const products = [ { id: 1, name: "Mouse", inStock: true }, { id: 2, name: "Keyboard", inStock: false }, { id: 3, name: "Monitor", inStock: true } ]; const available = products.filter(product => product.inStock); ``` --- ## 3. `reduce()` `reduce()` walks through an array and builds one final value. ```javascript const numbers = [10, 20, 30]; const total = numbers.reduce( (sum, number) => sum + number, 0 ); console.log(total); // 60 ``` The second argument, `0`, is the initial accumulator value. Think of the accumulator as a box that changes as we move through the array. ```text start: 0 + 10 = 10 + 20 = 30 + 30 = 60 ``` --- ## 4. Reduce with objects ```javascript const cart = [ { name: "Mouse", price: 45, qty: 2 }, { name: "Cable", price: 15, qty: 3 } ]; const total = cart.reduce( (sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0 ); console.log(total); // 135 ``` --- ## 5. The methods together This is common in dashboards: ```javascript const completedScores = students .filter(student => student.completed) .map(student => student.score); const total = completedScores.reduce( (sum, score) => sum + score, 0 ); ``` The data flows through a pipeline: ```text all students ↓ filter completed students ↓ map scores ↓ reduce total ``` --- ## 6. Do not mutate arrays This is dangerous with React state: ```javascript cart.push(product); // ❌ mutates existing array ``` Prefer: ```javascript setCart(previous => [ ...previous, product ]); ``` Remove: ```javascript setCart(previous => previous.filter(item => item.id !== id) ); ``` Update: ```javascript setCart(previous => previous.map(item => item.id === id ? { ...item, qty: item.qty + 1 } : item ) ); ``` --- ## 7. Common beginner differences ### `map()` ```javascript [1, 2, 3].map(x => x * 10); // [10, 20, 30] ``` ### `filter()` ```javascript [1, 2, 3].filter(x => x > 1); // [2, 3] ``` ### `reduce()` ```javascript [1, 2, 3].reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0); // 6 ``` Ask yourself: ```text Need a new value for every item? → map Need only some items? → filter Need one final result? → reduce ``` --- ## 8. React rendering example ```jsx function OrderSummary({ cart }) { const total = cart.reduce( (sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0 ); return (

    Order

      {cart.map(item => (
    • {item.name}: {item.qty} × ${item.price}
      • ))}
    Total: ${total}
    ); } ``` This is the foundation for many shopping carts, scoreboards, reports, and analytics screens. --- ## 9. Empty arrays Always consider the empty-array case. ```javascript [].reduce((sum, number) => sum + number, 0); // 0 ``` The explicit initial value makes the behavior predictable. For `map()`: ```javascript [].map(x => x * 2); // [] ``` For `filter()`: ```javascript [].filter(Boolean); // [] ``` --- ## Mini practice Given: ```javascript const marks = [80, 40, 95, 60]; ``` Find students above 50: ```javascript marks.filter(mark => mark > 50); ``` Double all values: ```javascript marks.map(mark => mark * 2); ``` Find the total: ```javascript marks.reduce((sum, mark) => sum + mark, 0); ``` Further reading: - React: Rendering Lists — https://react.dev/learn/rendering-lists - React: Updating Arrays in State — https://react.dev/learn/updating-arrays-in-state - W3Schools: React tutorial — https://www.w3schools.com/react/ - GeeksforGeeks: Getting Started with React — https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/reactjs/getting-started-with-react/
